newsitem.title: UK: Dlr battles on in Europe with eyes riveted to FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Dlr battles on in Europe with eyes riveted to FOMC.

text.p: The dollar struggled to regain its poise against the yen in late European trade, fighting uncertainty over U.S. interest rate policy and speculation about higher Japanese rates.

All were riveted to the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting which started earlier, with the market almost evenly split on the prospects of a 25-basis-point hike in the federal funds rate. Results of the meeting are expected after European trade winds down today, sometime after 1800 GMT.
In the meantime, dollar/yen was trying to claw back after dropping to a five-month low earlier but the going was tough.
Traders said that at the moment, the mood seemed to be one of cashing in on any signs of dollar recovery.

"Japanese funds have a lot of long dollar positions out there to worry about. They wanted to close out at higher levels and haven't been able to, so until they bail out, the dollar's going to remain offered," said one trader at a U.S. bank here.

The dollar slid to 111.98 yen in early European trade, trading below 112 for the first time since December 6 last year. It had recovered to 113.65/75 by 1525 GMT, but was still far below its late Monday European level of 115.93/03. Against the mark, it was at 1.6947/52 against 1.7101/06.

Dollar sentiment was severely hit by speculation of a rise in Japanese interest rates in the near future. This was fuelled by media reports that a committee of Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) was considering asking for a rise in the official discount rate, which has been at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995.
LDP officials were later quoted by Jiji news agency as saying now was not the time to tighten Japan's credit policy.
But expectations of a shrinking in the US-Japan yield gap -- a major engine of dollar/yen's rally which lasted until early this month -- lingered on, though some said it was premature.

"They (the reports) say the LDP's reason for asking for a rate hike was related to the change in Japan's foreign exchange laws, but that seems a rather weak motive," said Toshiyuki Suzuki, market economist at Sanwa Bank in London.

"There's also the argument of raising interest rates to help individuals and institutions who depend on interest rate income, but on the other hand, it will be very tough for Japanese banks unless interest rates are kept low," Suzuki said.
Meanwhile, analysts said that even if the Fed does decide to raise interest rates today, this will provide only a temporary boost for the dollar.
"If the Fed does raise rates, initially it will be moderately positive for the dollar, but I don't think it will last," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank here.

"It will create expectations that there won't be another move for at least another three months. And that will provide a window for the negative implications for the dollar in Europe and Japan to develop," Schmidt said.
Meanwhile, mark/yen also took a beating due to the yen's strength, dropping to a 20-month low of 66.43 yen. It recovered to 67.10/13 but was still below late Monday's 67.85/90.

On the European crosses, the mark sank to a six-and-a-half month low against the Swiss franc as the dollar's tumble against the yen sparked a flight into the Swissie, a traditional safe-haven currency.
Mark/Swiss dropped to a low of 82.87 centimes but later recovered to 82.97/99. It was at 83.60/65 in late European trade on Monday.
The British pound was range-bound against the mark and dollar, trading at 2.7853/63 marks and $1.6437/42 against Monday's 2.8000/10 and $1.6368/73.
